How to submit music to radio stations in Australia

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 2 min read Country & market guides

On this page
  • The Australia radio map
  • Where independent artists fit
  • Build a qualified Australia submission list
  • Pitch with market context
  • Rights, privacy, and outreach rules
  • A six-week campaign rhythm

Australia's independent-radio pathway is shaped by strong community broadcasting, national youth and public networks, regional stations, specialist presenters, and locally focused programs. Submission portals can be important, but they do not replace program-level research or guarantee that a track fits.

The Australia radio map

Community broadcasters and specialist programs offer decentralized access; national youth and public services use more structured discovery and programming systems; commercial and regional stations vary in how much music is selected locally.

  • Community stations and locally produced specialty shows
  • Youth and public-radio discovery routes that publish artist guidance
  • Regional programs where an artist has a genuine touring or community tie
  • Genre presenters and active online broadcasters
  • Commercial music teams only when the format and evidence justify the target

Where independent artists fit

Australian artists should map hometown, state, tour markets, community language or culture, and genre. Overseas artists need a strong program match, Australian collaborator, label connection, audience evidence, or confirmed dates rather than a generic international pitch.

The useful unit of research is often the individual show, not the parent network. Search schedules and recent playlists for genre programs, local-music blocks, emerging-artist features, and presenters who demonstrably play releases like yours.

Build a qualified Australia submission list

  1. Choose one release, one genre lane, and the regions where you have a credible audience or live plan.
  2. Separate national networks, local broadcasters, student/community stations, and online shows; they have different decision paths.
  3. Read each official submission policy and capture the required format, current contact, source URL, and verification date.
  4. Listen to or inspect a current playlist before deciding the station is a fit.
  5. Start with twenty to forty highly qualified prospects and expand only when the response data supports it.

A contact database is a research starting point, not proof of current acceptance. Staff and policies change; verify every priority contact against the station's own website before sending.

Pitch with market context

Lead with the exact program fit and include city/state or touring context where true. Make Australian release timing and availability clear, because overseas campaigns often create confusion about dates and rights territories.

Keep the first email under about 150 words. Include one stream, release date, concise genre description, and the exact program fit. Do not attach large audio files unless requested. If you have no genuine connection to a locality, lead with programming fit rather than inventing one.

Rights, privacy, and outreach rules

Australia's Spam Act regulates commercial electronic messages and emphasizes consent, sender identification, and functional unsubscribe processes. Use published submission channels where available, keep a suppression list, and do not harvest addresses or disguise promotional messages.

This is general campaign guidance, not legal advice. Use truthful sender details, identify the purpose of the email, retain suppression records, and follow the recipient's published process. Never buy guaranteed spins: legitimate programmers retain editorial control, and undisclosed payment for airplay can create serious legal and reputational risk.

A six-week campaign rhythm

  • Weeks −3 to −2: verify contacts, finalize the radio edit and one-sheet, and begin priority pitches.
  • Week −1: send the second researched wave; answer asset requests promptly.
  • Release week: notify relevant presenters once and monitor public playlists.
  • Week +1: send one concise follow-up where permitted.
  • Weeks +2 to +3: thank confirmed supporters, log results, and stop contacting nonresponders.

Frequently asked questions

Can an overseas artist submit music to radio in Australia?

Yes, where the genre program accepts international music or there is a real Australian connection. Check eligibility for local and national discovery programs before submitting.

What kind of radio should I target first in Australia?

Community and specialist shows with current playlists are the most directly researchable. Follow any official national discovery route exactly, and treat commercial rotation as a later-stage objective.

Can I send one bulk email to every station?

No. Station policies, applicable marketing laws, and basic professional etiquette all favor relevant, identified outreach. Build a small list, use the station's published route, personalize each message, and honor opt-outs immediately.
